sources.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
sources.text: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next? Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore. sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC
sources.text: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
sources.text: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips. But AI models are now so good at read

stories.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
stories.summary: We built agent evals to test how effective coding agents are at using Together AI. Small fixes to our docs, skills, and API errors lifted task completion rate from 75% to 97%.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
sources.text: Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI. It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned. Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint. By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example: List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents. After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways: Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th: When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it. Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back. After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts: Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking. We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency. To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity: Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier? List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled. Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page. The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available. More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap. To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill).

sources.name: Microsoft Research
sources.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
sources.text: By Aaron J. Li , Research Intern Weijia Xu , Senior Researcher Chandan Singh , Staff Research Scientist Zixiao Chen Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher Bin Yu , Professor Ion Stoica , Professor Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President

stories.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
sources.text: Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: OpenRouter Vision Models in Roboflow
sources.text: To compare OpenRouter vision models, run them side by side on your own images in Roboflow Workflows: connect one image to several OpenRouter blocks, switch models by changing the model ID, and compare answers, token counts, and response time in a single run. Add RF-DETR to detect and crop objects before the VLM call, then deploy the same pipeline through the Serverless API or on live video streams. Testing a vision-language model from another provider often means changing your code before you can try it on an image. OpenRouter gives you access to hundreds of models through one API. In Roboflow Workflows , you can run models in a visual pipeline. We'll build a workflow that sends the same image to three vision models and see how their answers differ. We'll also compare response times and check the input and output token counts. OpenRouter offers more than 300 models from different providers. Some of these are vision-language models (VLMs) , which accept images along with text prompts to analyze visual content. For example, a VLM can read text on a product package or identify its product category. It can also describe the objects in a scene. The accuracy of the result depends on the model and the image. Working with providers separately means managing different API keys and request formats. You could also need to change how your code reads their responses. Providers can handle failed requests differently, which affects how you write retry logic. OpenRouter gives you a common way to send requests to supported models. You can switch between vision models by changing the model ID instead of rewriting the integration. Roboflow Workflows is a visual editor where you can connect computer vision models with processing steps. Start by creating a new Workflow in your Roboflow workspace with an image input. Add the OpenRouter block to the pipeline and connect it to the image input. Then connect the OpenRouter block to Outputs to return the model's response. Click the OpenRouter block to open its settings. For this example, I selected Amazon Nova Pro (amazon/nova-pro-v1) in the Model ID field. The prompt tells the model what to look for in the image, such as text printed on product packaging. You can adjust the temperature to control how much responses vary and set max tokens to limit the length of the output. Reasoning effort controls how much reasoning a model uses, if supported. The privacy level setting lets you choose how providers can handle your request data. By default, Roboflow's OpenRouter block uses a Roboflow-managed API key, with usage charged through Roboflow credits. If you want to be billed directly by OpenRouter instead of using Roboflow credits, enter your personal OpenRouter API key in the block's API Key field. Depending on the model, the OpenRouter block can handle open prompts, optical character recognition ( OCR ), visual question answering , short and detailed image captions, single-label and multi-label classification , object detection, and structured JSON answers. I tested three of these tasks with Amazon Nova Pro using a fictional Northfield Pantry granola package. I uploaded the packaging image and asked the model to read the printed text. It correctly recognized the product name, ingredients, 340 g weight, lot code NP-2047, and best-before date 2027-08-14. For classification, I provided a list of categories and possible labels. The model selected breakfast cereal as the primary category. It also assigned breakfast food, contains almonds, and honey-flavored as additional labels. Single-label classification selects one category, while multi-label classification can return several. I also asked the model to extract product_name, brand, and quantity. It returned Honey Almond Granola, Northfield Pantry, and 340 g in a JSON-formatted string. These values could be used to fill product details in an inventory system. To compare three vision models, I used the same image and prompt for each one. This let me compare their answers and token usage under similar conditions. I reused the fictional Northfield Pantry granola package image. It has a clear product name and several printed details that the models can read. I created a new Workflow with one image input and three OpenRouter blocks. Each block connects directly to the same image input, allowing the models to process it independently. Connect each model's response and token counts to Outputs. Give each output a separate name so the results are easy to identify. For this comparison, I selected three vision models from different providers: All three blocks used Open Prompt, a temperature of 0.1, and a maximum of 300 output tokens.
